metadata.title: How Does Claude Tell Whether a Bond Is Rich or Cheap?
metadata.purpose: Answer whether Claude judges a bond's richness or cheapness by trading feel, or by running a fixed computed comparison across price, curve, spread, and stress scenario. Lands the carry-out that a rich-or-cheap read is a computed number waiting for a trader's decision, not Claude's own call.
metadata.source_note: Source sheet's narration carries real skill-specific facts (not unfilled template placeholders) -- see QUESTION.md. Facts preserved: the bond-relative-value skill performs relative value analysis on bonds by combining pricing, yield curve context, credit spreads, and scenario stress testing; used for richness/cheapness, spread decomposition, bond comparison, and rate-shock scenarios. Register re-registered Teardown -> Plain; source's B03 design-tell verdict became a plain mechanism + both-directions beat; a wrong-guess beat and an anchor (a ten-year corporate bond, +40bp over curve: priced -> curve read -> spread decomposed -> stress-tested -> a computed read, waiting) were added per hai-simple's Phase 1 structure, since the source's Teardown shape carried neither.

beats.narration_text: You'd guess Claude reads a bond and calls it rich or cheap on feel, the way a trader would. It doesn't — it runs a fixed procedure. I'm Liam, in for Bear; let's take that procedure apart.

shot.new_visual_element: Writer types 'Which bond is rich or cheap -- by feel?', hesitates on 'feel', corrects to 'a curve', lands the real question

props.text:
Which bond is
rich or cheap —
by feel?

beats.note: B00 is Remotion (BrutalistHesitantWriter) per hai-simple SKILL.md WRITER LAW. TIMING LAW: 20-35 word narration + lead_silence_s 0.8 to give the typing a >=9s window; verify media/B00.mp4 >= 8s and that the correction ('feel' -> 'a curve') is visible on a late frame.

beats.narration_text: Here's what's actually happening. The natural read is that Claude brings a trader's feel to the bond — pattern recognition, market intuition. It doesn't. The skill runs a fixed comparison over four inputs: the bond's price, the yield curve it sits on, the credit spread over that curve, and a stress-tested rate shock. Take away the curve and there's nothing to spread against — the skill won't invent one. They optimized for a repeatable procedure; they gave up the trader's ability to work without a benchmark.

shot.new_visual_element: A trader's-feel figure struck through; a priced/curve/spread/stress checklist lit instead

production_viz.label: Feel, struck -- price/curve/spread/stress, lit
production_viz.mechanic: Left: a figure icon labelled 'TRADER'S FEEL' beside a thought-bubble of scattered decision marks. Right: a numbered card labelled 'PRICE / CURVE / SPREAD / STRESS'. The feel side dims and gets a terracotta strike; the procedure side stays lit. A final line reads 'no curve -- nothing to spread it against' and the figure does not reach for it.

beats.narration_text: Here's the machinery in order. Take the bond's price, put it against the yield curve, decompose the credit spread over that curve, then shock the whole thing with a stress-tested rate move. Watch the anchor: a ten-year corporate bond trading forty basis points over the curve. Price. Curve read. Spread decomposed. Stress run. Four stops, and the skill halts — cheap by eight basis points, waiting. No verdict on what to trade; that's the design choice.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR -- a ten-year corporate bond traveling priced -> curve read -> spread decomposed -> stress run, then stopping

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR -- one bond, four stops
production_viz.mechanic: THE ANCHOR. Four stacked cards labelled 'PRICED', 'CURVE READ', 'SPREAD DECOMPOSED', 'STRESS RUN'. A single highlighted token '10Y CORP +40BP' travels down through all four cards in turn, each lighting as it arrives. At the bottom, the token halts beside a label 'read: cheap 8bp -- waiting'. THIS EXACT COMPOSITION RETURNS, PAID OFF, AT B03.

beats.narration_text: The read is built — priced, curved, spread-decomposed, stress-tested. Now name the trade-offs. Cheap by the read isn't the same as worth buying: the read only reflects the curve you fed it, and a stale curve gives you a wrong read with the same confidence as a right one. Rich by the read isn't automatically avoid it: the stress scenario can still favor holding. This works if you value repeatable, auditable numbers; it fails if you need the skill to compensate for a bad input or make the call itself.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR RETURNS, resting at the read; splits into 'cheap is not worth buying' and 'rich is not avoid it'

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR RETURNS -- read, then split
production_viz.mechanic: THE B02 FOUR-CARD COMPOSITION RETURNS, identical placement, the token resting at the 'STRESS RUN' card beside 'read: cheap 8bp'. It shrinks and slides up. Two cards fade in beneath: left reads 'CHEAP: 8BP' with a checkmark, then a struck-through 'WORTH BUYING?' beneath it, labelled 'cheap is not worth buying'; right reads 'RICH' beside a faint 'stress favors holding' note, labelled 'rich is not avoid it'.

beats.narration_text: A rich-or-cheap read isn't Claude's call on what to buy — it's a computed number, built from price, the curve, the spread, and a stress test, waiting for the person who has to defend the trade.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude. Give it one bond — coupon, maturity, current price — and one yield curve as a series of maturities and yields. Ask it to run the bond-relative-value skill: decompose the spread over the curve, then stress-test it against a hundred-basis-point parallel shift. Then swap in a different curve for the same bond and watch how much the read moves. Go deeper: ask Claude what would make the second read the wrong one to trust. Liam, in for Bear.
